tracks.title: Python backend developer
tracks.description: From your first Python script to tested code that talks to a database.

nodes.note: How to study the rest of this track in half the time.
Learn it alongside Python: you'll use it every day.
Optional, but it makes slow code easy to spot.
Once your code has tests, learn to keep it easy to change.
Size a service, then make it survive real traffic.

tracks.title: Java & Spring backend developer
tracks.description: Modern Java and Kotlin, databases and tests, ending with production-ready Spring Boot services.

nodes.note: How to study the rest of this track in half the time.
Optional: many Spring teams write Kotlin.
Layers, ports and modules for services that grow.
Caches, queues and replicas for when one server isn't enough.

tracks.title: Thinking skills
tracks.description: Think clearly about anything: learn fast, reason logically, question claims, break problems down and get comfortable with numbers.

nodes.note: Start here: it makes every other course faster.
Uses the percentages and fractions from Everyday Math.
Optional: growth patterns, applied to code.

tracks.title: C# game developer
tracks.description: From your first program to games that feel right on every machine: the game loop, movement and collisions, enemy AI, pathfinding and smooth performance.

nodes.note: How to study the rest of this track in half the time.
C# reads almost like Java: learn to program here, then the game course switches you over.
Learn it alongside Java: every game project lives in version control.
Ratios and rates come back every frame as speed, time and distance.
Optional, but it explains why pathfinding and collision checks slow down.

tracks.title: Game engine programmer (C++)
tracks.description: What runs underneath a game engine: C++ memory and ownership, the cache, data-oriented design, custom allocators and a fixed-step main loop.

nodes.note: How to study the rest of this track in half the time.
Learn the game ideas first, in C#, before you manage memory yourself.
Engines live and die by how work grows with the number of objects.
What engines do underneath: memory, the cache and data-oriented design.
